passage: In the office of the housing society in Kochi, Francis, twenty-six, had come to pay the maintenance and found a notice on the board: "Domestic help must use the back stairs and keep their own cups." Urmila, who cleaned his flat twice a week, was waiting outside the office to collect a new entry card. Francis took the card and gave it to her. "Good morning, Urmila. Your pay went into your account on the first, as always." Then he filled two cups from the office water cooler and handed her one. The clerk raised an eyebrow. Francis said politely, "Same water, same cups. Could the notice be reconsidered?" Urmila hesitated, then drank. "Thank you," she said. The clerk sighed. "I'll put it on the agenda for the next meeting."

qa.q: What did the notice on the board say?
qa.a: The notice said that domestic help must use the back stairs and keep their own cups.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Francis hands her a cup?
qa.a: Urmila is probably surprised and a little unsure, since she hesitates before she drinks, and then grateful, since she says thank you.

qa.q: Which choice by Francis addressed the notice as well as his own conduct?
qa.a: Francis greeted Urmila by name, shared the same cup and water, and politely asked for the notice to be reconsidered, so the clerk agreed to put it on the agenda.

qa.q: How might the clerk see Francis's request?
qa.a: At first as odd, since the eyebrow goes up, but the clerk sighs and agrees to put it on the agenda, so the clerk takes it seriously.

grounding: A young adult pays on time, greets a domestic worker by name, uses the same cups and questions a rule that keeps her apart.

passage: Abhinav, I want to write this instead of saying it at breakfast, so it doesn't sound like a lecture. I noticed that when Kamla-ji comes to cook, we leave her tea in the steel tumbler on the kitchen shelf, apart from ours. I did it too for weeks because that's what I saw at home, and I never questioned it. Last month I asked her if she would like tea in a proper cup, and she looked surprised, then happy. I have started paying her on the first of every month and asking after her son's exams. It costs nothing. It changes the mood in the flat. I'm not saying you're wrong; I only wanted to share what I changed. Tea is on me tomorrow, all three of us. Darshan

qa.q: When has Darshan started paying Kamla-ji?
qa.a: Darshan has started paying her on the first of every month.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel about the old habit of the separate tumbler?
qa.a: Darshan feels a little uncomfortable about it, since Darshan did the same for weeks without questioning it, and hopeful about the change.

qa.q: Which choice by Darshan changed the mood in the flat?
qa.a: Darshan offered Kamla-ji tea in a proper cup, paid her on the first of each month and asked after her son's exams.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Possibly surprised and a little defensive, but the gentle wording, Darshan's admission of doing the same and the offer of tea make it easier to listen.

grounding: A young adult pays a domestic worker on time, offers the same cup and greets her as a person, and shares this gently with someone who shares the kitchen.

passage:
Ishita, when I moved into my first flat, I thought I'd be the good employer just by being polite. Turns out politeness isn't the same as fairness.
Sunita-didi came to clean on my second day. I said "please" and "thank you," and I felt very modern. Then my mother visited and put aside a separate steel cup for Didi. And I let it happen.
That week I also paid Didi four days late, because I forgot. When I finally paid, she said, "Didi, I had to borrow for my son's fees."
That landed like a slap. I sat down and fixed things. Salary on the first, every month, without fail. One set of cups for everyone. I learned her son's name.
My mother grumbled about the cups for a month. Then she started saving leftover sweets for Didi's son. That's it, really. I'm Himani, and that's what I learned.

qa.q: Why did Sunita-didi have to borrow?
qa.a: She had to borrow for her son's fees because Himani paid her four days late.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Sunita-didi mentioned borrowing?
qa.a: Himani felt ashamed and shocked; she says it landed like a slap.

qa.q: What changes did Himani make, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Himani paid on the first of every month, used one set of cups for everyone and learned her son's name, small daily acts that treat the helper with dignity.

qa.q: How might Sunita-didi feel after the changes?
qa.a: Sunita-didi would likely feel more respected and secure, knowing her pay will come on time and she isn't kept apart with a separate cup.

grounding: A young adult learns that paying on time, using the same cups and treating the helper as a person is where class prejudice continues or ends.

passage:
I shared a flat with Divyansh for a year, and I learned more from watching him with Tanvir-bhai than from anything he said.
Tanvir-bhai cooked for us four days a week. Every morning, Divyansh greeted him by name, asked about his knee, and made the first cup of tea for both of them. They drank from the same mugs as the rest of us.
On the first of every month, Divyansh put Tanvir-bhai's salary in his hand before breakfast. Once, when I forgot to pay my share on time, Divyansh paid it and then told me quietly, "He has rent too, you know."
When Tanvir-bhai's daughter passed her exams, Divyansh brought sweets and asked about her plans.
I don't know how Tanvir-bhai felt inside. But he laughed a lot in our kitchen, and he stayed with us longer than with anyone else on the floor.

qa.q: When did Divyansh pay Tanvir-bhai's salary?
qa.a: On the first of every month, before breakfast.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh have paid the narrator's share when it was late?
qa.a: He was concerned that Tanvir-bhai has rent too, and seemed to feel responsible for making sure he was paid on time.

qa.q: What does Divyansh do that others could learn from?
qa.a: He greets Tanvir-bhai by name, shares the same mugs, pays on time and cares about his family, showing respect in small daily ways.

qa.q: How might Tanvir-bhai see working in that flat?
qa.a: He seems to feel comfortable and valued, since he laughs often and stayed longer there than with anyone else on the floor.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young adult paying on time, sharing cups and greeting the cook as a person, showing daily conduct that ends class prejudice.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage:
First week. Deepika, twenty-five, newly married, noticed that Binita-didi, who washed dishes at her in-laws' house, was given tea in a chipped cup kept on a separate shelf. Deepika's mother-in-law said it was "how things are."
Second week. Deepika started making tea herself when Binita-didi arrived, in the same cups as the family. She asked about Binita-didi's daughter by name. Her mother-in-law raised her eyebrows but said nothing.
A month later. Binita-didi's pay was late again, because nobody had remembered. Deepika sat with her mother-in-law and said gently, "Ma, can I take charge of her pay? I'll give it on the first." Her mother-in-law hesitated, then agreed.
That day, Deepika quietly moved the chipped cup to the back of the cupboard. Later, she noticed her mother-in-law serving Binita-didi tea herself, in a family cup.

qa.q: Where was Binita-didi's cup kept?
qa.a: It was kept on a separate shelf, a chipped cup.

qa.q: How might Deepika's mother-in-law have been feeling when she raised her eyebrows?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little uncomfortable, since Deepika was quietly changing the way things were done in her house.

qa.q: What made Deepika's approach work?
qa.a: She changed things through small daily acts and gentle requests rather than arguments, which gave her mother-in-law time to adjust.

qa.q: How might Binita-didi feel when she is served tea in a family cup?
qa.a: Binita-didi might feel respected and included after being set apart for a long time.

grounding: Over a month, a young adult offers dignity, pays on time and shares cups with a domestic worker, and slowly shifts the household's habits.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: Ishita, sit, I'll tell you about Kamla-bai while the rice cooks. I was twenty-four and had just taken my first flat in Nagpur. In the house I grew up in, a separate steel cup for the helper hung on a nail by the back door. The first morning Kamla-bai came, I reached for that kind of cup out of habit, and then I stopped. I poured her tea into the same blue mugs I used. She held hers a long moment before drinking. I paid her on the first of every month, never the fifth, and I learnt her grandson's name. Small things. Eleven years she worked with me. When I moved away, she came to the station with laddoos. Remember that when you set up your own house, beta: your Vinita Maasi learnt it from a cup.

qa.q: On which day of the month did Vinita pay Kamla-bai?
qa.a: She paid her on the first of every month, never the fifth.

qa.q: Why did young Vinita stop reaching for the separate cup, and what does that suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seems to have felt uncomfortable, even a little ashamed, at copying an old habit that treated a person as lesser.

qa.q: Which small choice in the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Pouring tea into the same mugs mattered most because it showed daily respect, and paying on time and learning her grandson's name kept that respect going.

qa.q: How might Kamla-bai have felt holding the blue mug?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and quietly moved, as if being treated as an equal in a house was new to her.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who uses the same cups, pays on time and treats the domestic helper as a person, showing daily conduct is where class prejudice ends.
